--- title: "Multiverse" subtitle: "The curve of the claim and the class results" engine: knitr format: live-html: toc: true include-after-body: ../../_includes/track-choice.html webr: packages: - tinyplot - datawizard - purrr resources: - data/spec_curve.csv - data/class_results.csv execute: echo: false warning: false message: false bibliography: [../../references.bib, ../../references-new.bib] --- ::: {.cell} ::: This page holds the curve of the claim of the immigration-and-trust case and the live chart of the class results. The claim, in the wording that SCORE took from the paper of the original author (OA) [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope], is that "... concerns about the effect of immigration on the national community have a(n) \[reducing\] impact on trust in politics". The curve holds every specification that the [specification menu](menu.qmd) keeps for this claim, 192 in all, each fitted on the respondents of the course extract of the European Social Survey (ESS). A specification is one complete set of answers to the decisions of an analysis. Five decisions vary on the curve: the outcome (distrust of parliament, of politicians, of the legal system, or the mean of the three), the adjustment (no controls, the demographics, those with outlook and ideology, or all the controls of the paper), the weights (none, design weights, or design and population weights), the rule for unanswered items (every item answered, or the answered items) and the comparison within countries (an intercept for every country-round, or one for every country with a shift for every round), which gives 4 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 192 specifications. Every specification keeps the citizens of the 16 countries who do not belong to an ethnic minority, measures concern with the index of three items, leaves out respondents with a missing answer, clusters its errors by country and reports the coefficient in points of distrust per point of concern. The [decision map](map.qmd) sets out every decision, including the options that are not on the curve, with the reason for each. ```{=html}
Specification curve of the claim
192 specifications, with the published result, the reproductions, the five reanalyses and the replications
Each mark is one specification: a circle for p < 0.05 and a cross for p ≥ 0.05, with errors clustered by country and t on 15 degrees of freedom. All 192 specifications are circles. The tags mark the published result of the original author (OA 2012), the two SCORE reproductions from the ESS files, the five Multi100 analysts and the two SCORE replications on later rounds (SCORE 2010 and SCORE 2010–18), each placed by its coefficient; the replications come from new data. Click or tap a tag to hold its details open, and click again to release it. Colour by colours the marks by one decision and adds rows under the curve that show where the specifications using each option fall in the ranking; Show only keeps the specifications that use one option and fades the rest. Hover over or tap a mark for its details, or focus the chart and use the arrow keys.
Data: data/spec_curve.csv and data/reference_marks.csv, with their codebooks.
``` All 192 specifications lie above zero, in the direction of the claim, and all 192 have p < 0.05 with errors clustered by country, so every mark on the chart is a circle and the shaded band below zero is empty. The estimates run from 0.326 down to 0.117 points of distrust per point of concern. The reference specification, the one closest to the model of the paper, gives 0.175 (t = 18.04 on 15 df), against the 0.17 of Table 3 of the paper. ## Reading the curve {#reading} Each mark is one specification, and the marks are ranked by their estimate, from the largest coefficient on the left to the smallest on the right. The estimate is the change in distrust, on the scale of 0 (complete trust) to 10 (no trust at all), that goes with one more point of concern about immigration, on its own scale of 0 to 10, among respondents of the same country and round who are alike on the controls of the specification. This is the scale of the coefficient of 0.17 that the paper reports. A value above zero means that more concerned respondents distrust the institution more, the direction of the claim, and the shaded band below zero would hold the results that run against it. The shape of a mark gives its class at the 5% level, an open circle for p < 0.05 and a cross for p ≥ 0.05. The p-value comes from errors clustered by country, which allow the respondents of one country to be alike in every round, with a t distribution on 15 degrees of freedom for the 16 countries. On this curve the clustered t runs from 11.3 to 21.6, so that every specification clears the threshold by a wide margin and the shape carries no information; what varies between the specifications is the size of the coefficient. The pop-up of each mark gives two further tests, with conventional errors and with errors clustered by country-round, and the partial correlation by the rule of Multi100, which converts the conventional test. Choosing a decision under *Colour by* colours the marks by the option that each specification uses and adds a row for each option under the curve, with a tick at the rank of every specification that uses it, so that an option which pushes results towards one end of the curve shows as a bunched row. Colouring by the adjustment divides the curve into blocks. *Show only* keeps the specifications that use one option, fades the rest, and reports how many are shown and how many of them lie above zero with p < 0.05. The button above the chart downloads the data behind it, with the option codes that `try_spec()` takes as arguments. The share of specifications that agree with the claim describes this set of analyses. It is not the probability that the claim is true, a distinction that [section 6 of the multiverse module](../../companion/multiverse.qmd#sec-reading) explains. ## Reference marks {#reference-marks} Ten tagged marks come from outside the curve: the published result of OA, tagged OA 2012; the two SCORE reproductions, which rebuilt the data of the paper from the ESS files; the five reanalyses that Multi100 recorded, tagged by the identifiers of the analysts; and the two SCORE replications, which fitted the model to later rounds of the ESS and so come from new data. Each is drawn as an ordinary mark in ink, at the end of a thin line to a tag that holds its pop-up open when clicked, and each is placed by its coefficient in points of distrust per point of concern. The published result is placed by the 0.17 of Table 3 of the paper, the reproductions and the replications by the coefficients that SCORE published, and the five analyses by the course refits on the file that Multi100 gave the analysts, which reproduce four recorded statistics exactly and the fifth to within 0.1%. Each mark is classed by its own test as published or recorded, and all ten are circles. ::: {#tbl-marks .cell tbl-cap='The ten reference marks: the statistic as published or recorded, the respondents analysed, the coefficient by which the mark is placed, and the number of specifications on the curve with a larger coefficient. Sources: `data/reference_marks.csv`, `data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Mark Data Statistic Respondents Coefficient Larger on the curve
FQ1G7 rounds 1–4 F = 3151.34 77,384 0.235 104
6U3LL rounds 1–4 t = 46.625 72,733 0.191 140
SCORE 2010–18 new rounds t = 50.11 90,286 0.186 142
SCORE 2010 new rounds t = 21.1737 17,134 0.183 144
SCORE e48gd rounds 1–4 t = 42.148 68,113 0.181 144
N8P2J rounds 1–4 t = 42.1 68,113 0.181 144
SCORE jp7tr rounds 1–4 t = 41.583 69,522 0.178 146
OA 2012 rounds 1–4 SE printed as 0.00 110,732 0.170 152
456AD rounds 1–4 z = 43.14 85,241 0.157 156
LT39B rounds 1–4 z = 31.747 67,358 0.115 192
``` ::: ::: None of the ten is a point of the curve. The paper, the reproductions, N8P2J and 6U3LL fitted the multilevel model of the paper with its country-level variables, and the curve replaces the random intercepts with an intercept for every country-round, which gives almost the same coefficient on the same respondents. Fitted to the 69,522 respondents of the reproduction osf.io/jp7tr, the reference specification comes within 0.001 of its published coefficient, as the [case study](index.qmd#sec-course-rebuild) shows. These marks and the two replications sit between 0.170 and 0.191, at the upper end of the specifications that hold constant the controls of the paper, which run from 0.117 to 0.179; the remaining differences come from their samples and from how their files code the variables, as the case study explains. FQ1G7 held constant a short list of controls without the evaluations of the economy and of public services, and it sits among the specifications that hold constant outlook and ideology. 456AD and LT39B added satisfaction with the government to their controls, an option off the curve that lowers the coefficient, and LT39B measured concern with a single item, which lowers it further and places it at the very end of the curve. ## What moved the estimate {#shifts} Every option on the curve can be set beside the first option of its decision on twin specifications, which agree on every other decision, and @fig-shifts summarises what each option does to the estimate. Holding constant the controls of the paper instead of nothing lowers the coefficient by 0.140 on average (from −0.150 to −0.132 across its 48 pairs), and holding constant outlook and ideology by 0.076, while the demographics barely move it (−0.004). No option of any other decision moves a specification by more than 0.055 points. Distrust of politicians lies 0.046 below distrust of parliament on average, and the weights, the rule for unanswered items and the comparison within countries move the estimate by less than 0.01 on average. No option moves any specification across the 5% threshold. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![What each option on the curve does to the estimate, against the first option of its decision on twin specifications: the mean shift (point) and the smallest and largest shift (line), in points of distrust per point of concern. Source: `data/menu_deviations.csv`.](multiverse_files/figure-html/fig-shifts-1.png){#fig-shifts fig-alt='Dot-and-range chart of ten options. The controls of the paper shift the estimate by about −0.14 and outlook and ideology by about −0.08; politicians lie about −0.05 below parliament and the other outcomes about −0.025; the demographics, weights, answered items and country and round effects lie within about 0.01 of zero.' width=720} ::: ::: Split by decision, the variance of the 192 estimates falls almost entirely on the adjustment, which carries 91.6% of it, against 7.5% for the outcome, less than 1% for each of the other decisions, and 0.5% for the interactions between decisions. Without controls the estimates run from 0.253 to 0.326, with the demographics from 0.259 to 0.315, with outlook and ideology from 0.183 to 0.249, and with the controls of the paper from 0.117 to 0.179. The four blocks are answers to four readings of the claim rather than four noisy estimates of one quantity: whether the evaluations of the economy and of public services, which carry most of the last step, are common causes, steps on the path or consequences of both attitudes is a question for the causal graph, as the [specification menu](menu.qmd#adjustment) sets out. ## Inference with 16 countries {#inference} The paper prints a standard error of 0.00 for every coefficient of concern, so its tables give no test statistic, and the SCORE power analysis had to assume the largest error that would round to 0.00, 0.0049. @tbl-inference sets the reference specification under five rules of inference. The coefficient is the same under each, apart from the random-intercept model, which estimates it slightly differently, and only the uncertainty attached to it changes. ::: {#tbl-inference .cell tbl-cap='The reference specification (distrust of parliament, the controls of the paper, no weights, every item answered, an intercept for every country-round) under five rules of inference. Source: `data/display_inference.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Rule Coefficient SE t df p
Conventional errors 0.1753 0.0043 41.2 70,253 < 0.0001
Clustered by country-round 0.1753 0.0066 26.5 56 < 0.0001
Clustered by country (the curve) 0.1753 0.0097 18.0 15 < 0.0001
CR2 by country, Satterthwaite df 0.1753 0.0097 18.0 13.3 < 0.0001
Random intercepts (multilevel model) 0.1753 0.0043 41.2 70,298 < 0.0001
``` ::: ::: Conventional errors treat the 70,326 respondents as independent pieces of evidence, which gives t = 41.2. The random-intercept model of the paper gives the same t. Its intercepts absorb the differences in the average level of distrust between countries and between country-rounds, but the model still assumes that the association of concern with distrust is the same everywhere and that the respondents of one country-round are otherwise independent, and neither assumption holds. The correlation of concern with distrust of parliament runs from about 0.17 in Italy to 0.38 in Norway, and respondents of the same country share institutions, media and events that the controls do not capture. Errors clustered by country allow for both: they let the residuals of the respondents of one country be related in any way, across all of its rounds, and they are 2.3 times the conventional ones at the reference specification, and 1.7 to 7.9 times across the curve. Clustering by country-round gives a value in between, because it treats the rounds of one country as independent. The price of clustering by country is that the evidence on the uncertainty rests on 16 clusters, and with few clusters even clustered errors can be too small. The curve therefore tests each coefficient against a t distribution on 15 degrees of freedom rather than a normal one, and a second rule checks the result. The CR2 correction of @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard enlarges the residuals of each country according to how strongly that country pulls the fitted values towards its own respondents, so that a country with an unusual mix of respondents no longer hides part of its own error. Its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom then say how many countries' worth of information the data hold, a number that falls below 15 when a few countries carry most of it. At the reference specification the CR2 error is 0.00975 against 0.00972 for the rule of the curve, and the test gives t = 18.0 on 13.3 degrees of freedom (p < 0.0001), so the correction barely moves this result. The clustered t of the curve runs from 11.3 to 21.6, and no rule changes the verdict of any specification. In the [EU-frames case](../eu-frames/multiverse.qmd), whose predictor varies only between country-years, the same few-cluster correction decides whether the reproduced result is significant; here the predictor varies between respondents within every country-round, and the association is strong enough to clear any threshold. The standard error printed as 0.00 hides a clustered error of 0.0097 at the reference specification, 2.3 times the conventional error, which itself rounds to 0.00, so a reader of the paper could not judge how far the 16 countries limit the precision of the estimate. The [statistics module](../../companion/stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) treats inference with few clusters at more length. ## Beside the curve {#beside} ### Options off the curve {#options} Several options of the menu stay off the curve, because each answers another question, answers this one less well or checks an answer that the curve already holds. @tbl-options fits each of those that a linear model can fit alone, at the reference settings. ::: {#tbl-options .cell tbl-cap='The options off the curve that a linear model can fit, each changed alone from the reference specification, with the test of errors clustered by country (model-based for the random intercepts), and the shift from the reference specification. Source: `data/display_options.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Decision Option Judgement Coefficient Shift t Respondents
Respondents All respondents another question 0.175 −0.000 18.8 75,179
Measure of concern Economy item a weaker answer 0.121 −0.055 19.6 71,396
Measure of concern Cultural life item a weaker answer 0.119 −0.056 15.3 71,692
Measure of concern Place to live item a weaker answer 0.129 −0.046 15.6 71,687
Adjustment Paper and satisfaction with the government a weaker answer 0.152 −0.024 14.7 69,771
Adjustment Paper without unhappiness a check 0.174 −0.001 17.7 70,402
Weights Post-stratification weights a check 0.177 +0.001 17.3 70,326
Weights Post-stratification and population weights a check 0.163 −0.012 14.5 70,326
Countries and rounds Pooled regression a weaker answer 0.184 +0.008 9.8 70,326
Vote controls Non-voters left out a weaker answer 0.173 −0.002 19.2 58,038
Countries and rounds Random intercepts a check 0.175 +0.000 41.2 70,326
``` ::: ::: The single items of concern lower the coefficient most, by about a third, because a single item measures the attitude with more random error than the mean of three, which pulls a coefficient towards zero. Satisfaction with the government lowers it by 0.024, because it is very nearly an evaluation of the institutions that the outcome asks about. The pooled regression, without intercepts for groups, raises it to 0.184, and its t falls to 9.8, because the differences between countries add to the association and to the noise around it. Every other option moves the estimate by less than 0.015. ### Leaving out one country {#loo} With 16 countries, one of them could carry the result. @fig-loo refits the reference specification 16 times, each time without one country. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The reference specification refitted without each country in turn, with 95% confidence intervals from errors clustered by the remaining 15 countries (t on 14 df). The dashed line is the estimate on all 16 countries. Source: `data/display_loo.csv`.](multiverse_files/figure-html/fig-loo-1.png){#fig-loo fig-alt='Dot-and-interval chart of 16 rows, one for each country left out. Every estimate lies between about 0.169 and 0.178, close to the dashed line at 0.175, with intervals from about 0.15 to 0.20.' width=672} ::: ::: The estimate moves only between 0.169 (without NO) and 0.178 (without PT), so no single country carries the result. ### Between countries {#between} Every specification of the curve compares respondents within countries. Countries differ as well, and @fig-between sets the mean concern of each country against its mean distrust of parliament. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean concern about immigration and mean distrust of parliament in the 16 countries, averaged over the rounds in which each took part (labels), and in the 60 country-rounds (grey points), among the respondents of the paper, with design weights. Source: `data/display_country_means.csv`.](multiverse_files/figure-html/fig-between-1.png){#fig-between fig-alt='Scatter plot of 16 country labels and 60 grey points. Mean concern runs from about 3.9 to 6.6 and mean distrust from about 3.6 to 6.2; the points rise from lower left to upper right, with Greece most concerned and Portugal most distrustful.' width=672} ::: ::: Across the 60 country-rounds, mean concern and mean distrust of parliament correlate at 0.69. Where citizens worry more about immigration, they also distrust their parliament more, but countries differ in their histories of immigration, in their politics and in the performance of their governments, and any of these can move both means at once. The claim is about respondents, so the curve sets these differences aside, and the pooled regression, which mixes them in, is a weaker answer. The paper itself reads the correlation of national means as supporting evidence (p. 213), and its multilevel model estimates the country-level variables alongside the individual coefficient. ## Robustness and replication {#replication} Within the original data the claim holds under every defensible analysis that the course can fit. All 192 specifications are positive and significant, from 0.117 to 0.326 points of distrust per point of concern, and the decisions of the menu change the size of the coefficient and never its sign or its verdict. Two SCORE replications asked the same question of new respondents, in later rounds of the ESS. The replication on round 5 (2010), with 13 of the 16 countries and post-stratification weights, found 0.183 on 17,134 respondents (t = 21.17), and the replication on rounds 5–9 (2010–2018), with the three-level model, found 0.186 on 90,286 (t = 50.11). Both met the criterion of SCORE, and both lie within 0.01 of the reproductions of the original model. A curve shows how much a conclusion depends on the decisions of the analysis, given one sample, and a replication shows whether the same analysis finds the same answer in another. This case has both, unlike the [housing-audit case](../housing/multiverse.qmd#robustness), whose claim survived every analysis of the original data and failed in a new experiment. Neither, however, speaks to the causal reading of the claim. Reverse causation, from distrust to concern, and common causes that no specification holds constant would produce a stable association across specifications and across rounds just as an effect of concern on distrust would, which is why the causal graph of Task 2 asks what a set of controls can and cannot settle. ## Class results {#class-results} The live chart below shows the results that the class submits, over the curve of 192 specifications. Pressing *Run Code* runs the `refresh_multiverse()` function, which downloads the latest submissions and draws them over the curve. The marks of the curve stay faint, so that the class results lead, and the reference marks are left to the chart at the top of the page. Each submission sits at the rank of its specification on the curve and at the coefficient that it reports, and it is classed by looking its specification up in the curve file: a circle if the matching specification has p < 0.05, as all 192 do, and a cross if it has not. An open green circle is an *explored* specification, one that you tried with `try_spec()` in Task 4 and submitted after seeing its result. A filled black circle is a *declared* specification, the one that you fixed in your preregistration in Task 5 before running it. A submission whose label names no specification of the curve is not drawn, and a line under the chart counts such submissions. Each submission also carries the tag that `submit_exploration()` and `report_result()` print, such as `amber-otter-42`, and your two submissions share it. The lines printed under the chart give each mark by its number, with its tag, its specification and its statistics. Typing your tag into the `my_tag` line of the cell below and pressing *Run Code* draws your marks in orange, joined in the order in which you submitted them. ::: {.cell autorun='true'} ```{webr} #| label: live-multiverse-setup #| include: false #| autorun: true # Class submissions are served as CSV by a Cloudflare Worker in front of the # Google Sheet of the results Form; when the Worker cannot be reached the # chart falls back to the committed data/class_results.csv. The Sheet is shared # by the cases of the course, so only the rows whose label carries the word # "trust" after the tag are read. The chart is drawn with tinyplot # (McDermott, Arel-Bundock and Zeileis; CRAN, doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.tinyplot), # the rows are handled with datawizard and purrr, and the labels are parsed # with the regular expressions of base R, so that participants download little. # ---- The Worker of the class results: replace this one line for a Form of its own worker_url <- "https://class-results.chris-moreh.workers.dev/" plain <- "#1f5fa8"; ink <- "#1d2733"; green <- "#009E73"; orange <- "#E69F00" grey_mid <- "#8a929a" phase_levels <- c("explored (Task 4)", "declared (Task 5)") # The backdrop is the curve of 192, ranked from the largest coefficient, as on # the chart at the top of the page. curve <- utils::read.csv("data/spec_curve.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |> # r-style: keep – base reader, nothing to download datawizard::data_arrange(c("-b", "spec_id")) |> datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n(), sig = p < 0.05, sig_f = factor(sig, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))) axis_codes <- c("outcome", "controls", "weights", "items", "fe") curve_key <- purrr::pmap_chr(curve[axis_codes], \(...) paste(..., sep = "|")) # A trust label, as the submission helpers write it: # explore: [amber-otter-42] trust outcome=parliament controls=paper weights=none items=complete fe=country_round # The phase and the tag are read when present. Labels of the other cases # carry no "trust" at that place and are left out. The five decisions are # key=value pairs in any order; a label that does not name each of them exactly # once, or carries anything else, returns NA on every axis and so matches nothing. trust_pattern <- "^((explore|declared): )?(\\[([a-z0-9-]{1,24})\\] )?trust( (.*))?$" parse_axes <- function(rest) { none <- setNames(rep(NA_character_, length(axis_codes)), axis_codes) pairs <- regmatches(rest, gregexpr("[a-z_]+=[a-z_]+", rest))[[1]] keys <- sub("=.*$", "", pairs) if (length(pairs) != length(axis_codes) || anyDuplicated(keys) > 0 || !setequal(keys, axis_codes)) return(none) if (nzchar(trimws(gsub("[a-z_]+=[a-z_]+", "", rest)))) return(none) setNames(sub("^.*=", "", pairs), keys)[axis_codes] } read_clean <- function(path) { d <- utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE, colClasses = "character") # r-style: keep – base reader, nothing to download names(d) <- tolower(trimws(names(d))) # tolerate "B", " spec ", etc. d } # my_tag is the tag that submit_exploration() and report_result() print. It is # reduced exactly as .clean_tag() in the submission helpers reduces a nickname # (transliterated to ASCII, lower case, single hyphens, at most 24 characters), # so that a nickname typed as the participant first wrote it still matches. clean_my_tag <- function(x) { if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x[1])) return("") x <- gsub("ß", "ss", chartr("ȘșȚț", "SsTt", trimws(as.character(x[1])))) ascii <- suppressWarnings(iconv(x, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")) if (!is.na(ascii)) x <- ascii x <- gsub("^-+|-+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x))) gsub("-+$", "", substr(x, 1, 24)) } fmt_num <- function(x, d) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)) fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", sprintf("p = %.3f", p)) # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download as_num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)) # The trust rows of the class CSV, parsed and looked up on the curve. Returns # the rows to draw, each with a line that describes it, the number of trust # rows, and the number that name no specification of the curve (or carry no # coefficient) and are therefore not drawn. prepare_class <- function(cls, my_tag = "") { empty <- list(points = NULL, n_trust = 0L, n_off = 0L) if (is.null(cls) || nrow(cls) == 0 || !("spec" %in% names(cls))) return(empty) spec_raw <- trimws(ifelse(is.na(cls$spec), "", cls$spec)) # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download m <- regmatches(spec_raw, regexec(trust_pattern, spec_raw)) is_trust <- lengths(m) > 0 if (!any(is_trust)) return(empty) cls <- cls[is_trust, , drop = FALSE] m <- m[is_trust] n <- nrow(cls) part <- function(k) purrr::map_chr(m, \(g) g[k]) ph <- ifelse(part(3) == "explore", "explored", "declared") # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download tg <- ifelse(nzchar(part(5)), part(5), NA_character_) # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download rest <- part(7) hit <- rest |> purrr::map(parse_axes) |> purrr::map_chr(\(a) paste(a, collapse = "|")) |> match(curve_key) b <- as_num(cls$b) drawn <- !is.na(hit) & !is.na(b) stat_txt <- function(i) { st <- as_num(cls$t[i]) if (is.na(st)) return("") d_f <- if ("df" %in% names(cls)) as_num(cls$df[i]) else NA if (is.na(d_f)) paste0(", t = ", fmt_num(st, 2)) else paste0(", t = ", fmt_num(st, 2), " on ", d_f, " df") } info <- purrr::map_chr(seq_len(n), \(i) paste0( "#", i, " (", ph[i], ")", if (is.na(tg[i])) "" else paste0(", tag ", tg[i]), ": b = ", fmt_num(b[i], 3), " points per point", stat_txt(i), if (is.na(hit[i])) "" else paste0(", on the curve ", fmt_p(curve$p[hit[i]]), if (curve$sig[hit[i]]) " (circle)" else " (cross)"), "; ", rest[i] )) points <- data.frame(n_lab = paste0("#", seq_len(n)), # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download phase = factor(ifelse(ph == "explored", phase_levels[1], phase_levels[2]), # r-style: keep – base, nothing to download levels = phase_levels), tag = tg, b = b, rank = curve$rank[hit], sig = curve$sig[hit], info = info, mine = nzchar(my_tag) & !is.na(tg) & tg == my_tag, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)[drawn, , drop = FALSE] list(points = points, n_trust = n, n_off = sum(!drawn)) } # The chart: the curve faint behind, a submission at the rank of its # specification and at the coefficient that it reports, a circle where that # specification has p < 0.05 and a cross otherwise, open green for explored # and filled black for declared, numbered in the order of submission. The # marks of the tag typed into the live cell are ringed in orange and joined in # the order of submission. The lines printed under the chart describe each mark. draw_class_chart <- function(cls, my_tag = "") { pts <- cls$points has_pts <- !is.null(pts) && nrow(pts) > 0 ylim_lo <- if (has_pts) min(0, min(pts$b) - 0.02) else 0 ylim_hi <- if (has_pts) max(0.4, max(pts$b) + 0.02) else 0.4 off_txt <- paste0(cls$n_off, " of ", cls$n_trust, " submission(s) name no specification of the curve of 192 and are not drawn.") sub_txt <- if (!has_pts && cls$n_trust == 0) { "No submissions yet – press Run Code to refresh" } else if (!has_pts) { "No submission can be placed yet – press Run Code to refresh" } else if (any(pts$mine)) { paste0(nrow(pts), " class result(s) on the chart; tag ", my_tag, ": ", paste(pts$n_lab[pts$mine], collapse = ", ")) } else if (nzchar(my_tag)) { paste0(nrow(pts), " class result(s) on the chart; no mark carries the tag ", my_tag, " yet") } else { paste(nrow(pts), "class result(s) on the chart") } tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal") on.exit(tinyplot::tinytheme()) # an empty frame that sets the axes and carries the legend of the two phases; # tinyplot reads palette and legend as written, so they take values, not names tinyplot::tinyplot(b ~ rank | phase, data = data.frame(rank = 1, b = 0, phase = factor(phase_levels, levels = phase_levels)), # Until a Form of its own is created, the immigration-and-trust case shares the Form, the Sheet and the Worker that were set up for the EU-frames case. The cell above fetches the CSV in the browser, keeps only the rows whose free-text spec field carries the word `trust` after the tag, and falls back to the committed `data/class_results.csv`, which holds only the header row, when the Worker cannot be reached. The spec field carries the phase (`explore:` or `declared:`), the tag of the participant in square brackets, the word `trust` and the five decisions of the curve as `key=value` pairs, for example `explore: [amber-otter-42] trust outcome=parliament controls=paper weights=none items=complete fe=country_round`. Each submission is placed by the coefficient `b` that it carries, in points of distrust per point of concern, at the rank of its specification, and classed by the p-value of the matching row of `data/spec_curve.csv`. A trust label that does not name each of the five decisions exactly once, or that names an option off the curve, matches no row and is counted under the chart without being drawn. The housing-audit chart ignores trust rows, but the EU-frames chart reads every row of the shared Sheet and would draw them as unclassed diamonds, so clear the data rows of the Sheet before a delivery of any case. Replacing the Form means editing the `worker_url` line of the cell above and the configuration blocks of the workspace helpers and the browser lab; the setup note `facilitator/live-results-setup.md` in the repository lists the steps. ## References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} :::
